chapter.title: Keeping the keys: saving every good version with Git and GitHub

cards.body:
A careful contractor photographs every room each time a job is finished, dates the photos, and locks a copy in a cabinet across town. Knock down the wrong wall tomorrow, and you can rebuild to any photo.

*Git* is the camera on your computer. *GitHub* is the cabinet across town. **You keep every good version, so no mistake is permanent.**
cards.simpler:
Picture a careful builder who takes a photo of every room each time a job is done. He writes the date on each photo and locks a copy in a cabinet across town. If someone knocks down the wrong wall tomorrow, he can rebuild from any photo.

Git is the camera on your computer. GitHub is the cabinet across town. **You keep every good version, so no mistake is permanent.**

cards.prompt: Sunday night your to-do app worked, and you took a Git 'photo' of it. Monday you asked Claude for dark mode and now the page is blank. What can you do?

options.text: Go back to Sunday's photo and start Monday again
Nothing. Monday's changes replaced Sunday's for good
Wait. GitHub repairs broken pages overnight

whyNot.b: That's a folder without Git, not a folder with it: Git keeps every photo you took, so Sunday is still there.
whyNot.c: That's a storage cabinet, not a repair shop: GitHub holds copies of your photos, it never changes your code.

cards.reteach: Each photo is a full copy of the project at that moment. New work never deletes old photos. If today breaks, you ask for yesterday's photo and the whole folder goes back to that state.

cards.title: Commit: take the photo
cards.body:
*Git* is a free program that lives on your computer and remembers the history of one folder. A *commit* is one save point: a snapshot of every file, plus a short note you write about what changed.

You never type Git commands yourself. You tell Claude: "commit this with the message 'to-do list adds and deletes items'". Claude runs the commands and tells you when it's done.

**Commit when it works, not when you're tired.** Open the app, click around, see it behave, then take the photo. A photo of a broken room is a photo you'll never want to rebuild from.
cards.simpler:

You never type Git commands yourself. You tell Claude: "commit this with the message 'to-do list adds and deletes items'". Claude does it and tells you when it is done.

**Commit when it works, not when you're tired.** Open the app, click around, and watch it behave. Then take the photo. A photo of a broken room is one you will never want to rebuild from.

cards.title: Maya and the vanishing delete button
cards.body:
Tuesday, 9pm. Maya's to-do app adds and deletes tasks, so she tells Claude to commit it with the message "adds and deletes tasks". Wednesday she asks for drag-to-reorder. Claude edits 3 files, and the delete button disappears.

She types: "go back to the last commit". About 4 seconds later the delete button is back. So is Tuesday's app, exactly as it was. Drag-to-reorder is gone too, which she decides is fine, since it never worked anyway.
cards.simpler:
Tuesday, 9pm. Maya's to-do app can add and delete tasks. She tells Claude to commit it with the message "adds and deletes tasks". On Wednesday she asks for drag-to-reorder. Claude edits 3 files, and the delete button disappears.

She types: "go back to the last commit". About 4 seconds later the delete button is back. Tuesday's app is back too, exactly as it was. Drag-to-reorder is gone as well. She decides that is fine, since it never worked anyway.

cards.prompt: You asked Claude to make the header green. You opened the app. It's green and nothing else changed. What now?

options.text: Commit now with a message like 'header is green'
Keep going for 5 more features, then commit once to keep the history short
Don't commit yet. Commits are for when something breaks, as a record of the break

whyNot.b: That's one photo of 6 rooms, not 6 photos: if feature 4 breaks things, you can't go back to feature 3.
whyNot.c: That's a bug report, not a save point: you commit the working state so you have something good to return to.

cards.reteach: Small, working, checked: that's the moment to commit. Each commit is cheap and takes seconds. Many small photos let you go back to exactly the step before trouble started.

cards.title: Push: lock a copy across town
cards.body:
A commit lives only on your computer. Laptop stolen, coffee in the keyboard, and every photo goes with it. *Push* means uploading your commits to *GitHub*, a website that stores a copy of your project.

Tell Claude: "push this to GitHub". The first time, it will help you create a *repository*, which is just the storage space for one project on GitHub. After that, pushing is one line.

**Commit saves, push protects.** To go back, ask "show me the last 5 commits", then "go back to the one called 'adds and deletes tasks'". Anything unsaved since that commit is set aside, so commit first if you want to keep it.
cards.simpler:
A commit lives only on your computer. If your laptop is stolen or coffee spills on it, every photo goes with it. Push means uploading your commits to GitHub, a website that keeps a copy of your project.

Tell Claude: "push this to GitHub". The first time, it helps you create a repository. That is just the storage space for one project on GitHub. After that, pushing is one line.

**Commit saves, push protects.** To go back, ask "show me the last 5 commits", then "go back to the one called 'adds and deletes tasks'". Anything unsaved since that commit is set aside, so commit first if you want to keep it.

cards.body:
Dev pushed on day 1, then committed 12 times over 2 weeks and never pushed again. His laptop died on a Thursday. GitHub had the day 1 version: a blank page with a title.

Spot it by asking Claude "is everything pushed to GitHub?" or by opening your repository page in a browser and reading the date on the last change. If it's older than your last commit, push.
cards.simpler:
Dev pushed on day 1. Then he committed 12 times over 2 weeks and never pushed again. His laptop died on a Thursday. GitHub only had the day 1 version: a blank page with a title. Two weeks of work were gone.

You can spot this early. Ask Claude "is everything pushed to GitHub?" Or open your repository page in a browser and read the date on the last change. If that date is older than your last commit, push.

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'I committed 6 times today. If my laptop dies tonight, is my work safe?' What do you tell them?

options.text: Yes. Commits go to GitHub on their own
Only if they also pushed. Commits stay on the laptop until then
No. Commits are wiped when you close the terminal

whyNot.a: That's push, not commit: nothing leaves your computer until you ask Claude to push.
whyNot.c: That's a scratch file, not a commit: commits stay in the folder's history until you delete the folder itself.

cards.reteach: Two separate steps. Commit takes the photo and files it on your computer. Push carries copies to GitHub. Without the second step, one dead hard drive takes all 6 photos with it.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every time the app works, tell Claude to commit it with a note saying what changed, then push it to GitHub. **If tomorrow breaks it, go back to the last commit** and lose minutes instead of days.
cards.simpler: Every time the app works, tell Claude to commit it. Add a short note saying what changed. Then tell Claude to push it to GitHub. **If tomorrow breaks it, go back to the last commit.** You lose minutes of work instead of days. It is like saving a game before a hard level, so you can always try again from a safe spot.

cards.body: Open Claude Code in your project folder. Type: "commit everything with a clear message, then push to GitHub". Then open your repository page in a browser and check the date on the latest change.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in your project folder. Type: "commit everything with a clear message, then push to GitHub". Wait for Claude to say it is done. Then open your repository page in a browser and check the date on the latest change. It should be today. If it is, your work is safely stored in two places: your computer and GitHub.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now commit a working version, push it to GitHub, and roll back to yesterday's version when today's attempt goes wrong.
